P1.reason: A puts every statement in its own group, so it names no rules. B's groups, though imperfect, match recognisable rules: corridor, movement, two-step restriction, turns, winning.

differences.reason: Hurts: plus2 isolated from the succ chain and the two-square step that use it.
Hurts: one-step legality alone, separated from the clear and inside helpers it needs.
Hurts: two-step legality split from the fresh/stale tracking that defines its restriction.
Hurts: hold legality alone, not tied to its position-keeping effect.
Hurts: clear (no landing on other token) detached from the step moves it constrains.
Hurts: stale update fragmented from the rest of the no-double-two-step rule.
Hurts: one-step position update split from the other movement effects.
Hurts: turn alternation split across singletons instead of one turn-order rule.
Hurts: home separated from terminal and goal; the winning rule is scattered.
Hurts: termination by white alone, half of one end-of-game rule.
Hurts: each corridor square as a separate group buries the corridor-bounds rule.
Hurts: single succ fact; the forward ordering is one concept spread over seven groups.
Helps: square ordering with plus2; including next(at) for step(1) is a slight intrusion.
Helps: all inside facts together form the corridor-bounds rule.
Helps: token position updates plus starting squares form a coherent movement-effect group.
Helps: two-step legality with freshness tracking captures the no-repeated-two-step rule, missing stale updates.
Mixed: hold and wait gathered, but stale/fresh carry-over muddles it with the two-step rule.
Helps: reaching square 7, termination and goal form the clean winning rule.
Helps: turn alternation with initial control is exactly the turn-order rule.
Helps: the two roles together name the players.
Mixed: one-step with clear is good; stale statements 24 and 25 do not belong.
Mixed: two-step with clear and freshness is good, overlaps B4 and lacks 25.
